series.name: The Couples Therapist
series.tagline: Every fight is about something else.
series.concept: Dr. Kabir Mehta — 47, couples therapist in Bandra, Mumbai. Each episode: one couple, one fight, one Daniel Goleman EQ concept underneath. He thinks it's about money — it's about empathy. She thinks he doesn't care — he doesn't know how to show it. The therapist names the emotion they can't.

episodes.title: The Joint Account

slides.text:
Tuesday, 6 PM.

They sit down.

He takes the chair near the window.
She takes the other one.

There is a third chair between them — empty.

That's where the fight will sit.

He says: "I just want a joint account. We're married. It's basic."

She says: "I told you. I don't want one."

He says: "Then say why."

She says: "I don't know why."

She knows why.

What Rohan says:

"I just want a joint account."

What Rohan means:

"I don't know how else to ask if you trust me.

If you say yes to this one thing, I'll know we're okay."

What Meera says:

"I don't want one."

What Meera means:

"Two years ago I asked you for money to buy Mumma a saree.

You said: 'kitne ka?'

I said never mind.

I have not asked you for anything since."

Dr. Mehta opens his notebook.

Writes one word.

Looks up.

"Rohan," he says.

"When was the last time you had to ask someone for money?"

Rohan opens his mouth.

Then closes it.

He is twenty-one, in his father's study, asking for a college fee.

EMPATHY

Goleman: "The ability to know what another person feels — even when they cannot say it."

In marriage, empathy is not agreeing.

It is perceiving what your partner needs you NOT to ask.

Meera does not need a joint account.

Meera needs to never have to say 'kitne ka?' to anyone, ever again.

Rohan looks at Meera.

For the first time in the session, at her — not at his case.

"You said kitne ka," he says quietly.

"I did," she says.

"I will never say that to you again."

It is not a solution.

It is the first crack of light.

Next time on The Couples Therapist:

A husband and wife who have not had a fight in four years.

They eat dinner in silence.

He thinks they have grown peaceful.

She has been screaming inside the whole time.

Episode 2: The Silent Dinner.

episodes.synopsis: Rohan (banker, 35) and Meera (writer, 33) — six years married, South Bombay. He wants a joint account. She refuses. He thinks she doesn't trust him. The truth is older: last time she asked him for money to buy her parents an anniversary gift, he asked 'kitne ka?' in a particular tone. She froze. She'd rather earn less than ask permission. The fight is not about money. It is about dignity, and Rohan has never been asked to imagine that.
episodes.caption:
He thinks the fight is about a joint account. She thinks she doesn't know why she's saying no.

Two years ago she asked him for money to buy her mother a saree. He said 'kitne ka?' She said never mind. She has not asked him for anything since.

The fight is not about money. It is about dignity.

Daniel Goleman calls this empathy: the ability to perceive what your partner needs you NOT to ask.

Look at your last fight. What was it actually about?

episodes.title: The Silent Dinner
episodes.synopsis: Aarti (38) and Rajat (40), eighteen years married, Powai. They eat dinner without speaking. He thinks they've grown peaceful. She has been screaming inside for four years. Goleman: stonewalling is not calm — it is emotional flooding so severe the body has shut the mouth to protect the heart from going faster than it can survive.

episodes.title: The Wedding Photo
episodes.synopsis: A casual jab about her weight at a family lunch. The fight at home is about 'you never defend me.' It's actually about a single image: him not standing up, in front of his mother, again. Goleman: the amygdala fires before the cortex has time to consult. By the time the words arrive, the body has already chosen its enemy.

episodes.title: Her Promotion
episodes.synopsis: Karthik (36) and Divya (34), Andheri. She's been promoted to VP. He says he's proud. He's been picking small fights for three weeks — the dishwasher, the cab, the way she folded a shirt. He doesn't know why. Dr. Mehta asks him to name the feeling. He cannot. That is the diagnosis.

episodes.title: Phone Beside the Pillow
episodes.synopsis: Aman (29) and Tanu (28), young marriage in Worli. She says, 'It's been a long day.' He says, 'Mine too.' Goleman, drawing on Gottman: she made a bid. He returned with one of his own instead of receiving hers. They are not fighting. They are missing each other one sentence at a time, every night.

episodes.title: Two Years
episodes.synopsis: A couple in their late thirties who have not had sex in two years. Neither is angry. Both are ashamed. Neither knows the other is ashamed. The shame is the lock. The therapist's question: 'If you both knew the other was carrying this same weight, would you put it down together?'

episodes.title: The School Application
episodes.synopsis: A four-year-old's school application. The surface fight: Bishop Cotton vs a Marathi-medium school nearby. The real fight: whose childhood gets to win. He was the convent boy who didn't speak Marathi. She was the Marathi-medium girl who taught herself English from soap operas. They are not fighting about their daughter. They are fighting about which of them was unfairly raised.

episodes.title: The Other Number
episodes.synopsis: Six months after an affair. He has apologized. She has 'moved on.' Then in the session she rolls her eyes when he speaks. Goleman, citing Gottman's research: that single eye-roll is more dangerous than the affair. Contempt is not a feeling — it is a verdict, and verdicts end marriages.

episodes.title: The Long Distance
episodes.synopsis: He's in Bangalore for work. She's in Bombay. Marathi, an arranged match, two years in. He cannot say 'I miss you.' He says 'the WiFi here is bad.' The therapist makes him say one true sentence about how he feels. He cannot get the word out. When he does, he cries. Naming the emotion is the work — Goleman's most quoted finding from neuroscience: the act of putting feelings into words calms the amygdala.

episodes.title: The Outsider
episodes.synopsis: A Hindu-Muslim couple, fourteen years, two children. The current fight: which Eid the kids attend. The real fight: she has never felt fully seen by his mother. He has never asked his mother to try. Goleman: empathy is hardest where we most need it — across the lines our families drew before we were born.

episodes.title: Maa is Sick
episodes.synopsis: A husband whose mother is dying. A wife who has done six months of cooking, doctor visits, medicine schedules, hospital insurance forms. She is not angry that he is grieving. She is furious that he has not noticed she has been grieving alongside him — for him, for her own absent mother, for a life she did not sign up for. Empathy as the daily noticing of the unseen.

episodes.title: The Couple Everyone Loves
episodes.synopsis: Instagram-perfect. Their friends call them 'couple goals.' They have been planning to leave each other for almost a year. They came to therapy not to repair the marriage but to learn how to tell their parents it is over. Goleman: the highest-cost self-deception is the one your peer group reinforces.

episodes.title: Two Pink Lines
episodes.synopsis: She is pregnant. They did not plan it. He is certain — let's keep it. She is not. He thinks her hesitation is a rejection of him. It is not. The therapist holds the room while she finds the sentence: 'I love you and I am not ready and both of those are true.' Most marriages die on the rock of needing to be sure.

episodes.title: Just One Drink
episodes.synopsis: He drinks. She manages. Every evening is a negotiation neither of them named. The therapist asks the question that breaks them both: 'Whose feeling are you actually managing?' Goleman: when you make yourself responsible for another adult's emotion, you take from them the only thing that can change them — the consequence of feeling it themselves.

episodes.title: My Daughter
episodes.synopsis: Second marriage. His daughter from the first. Every fight starts with the daughter. Every fight is actually about: 'I gave up my old life for this and I do not feel chosen.' Goleman, citing Gottman: a complaint is about a behavior. A criticism is about a character. One can be repaired. The other corrodes.

episodes.title: Less Than Her
episodes.synopsis: She earns four times what he does. He says it does not bother him. His shoulders say something else. Until he can name it — out loud, to her, in this room — the unnamed shame runs the marriage from the basement. Goleman: feelings you do not name will be acted out instead of spoken.

episodes.title: Whose Diwali
episodes.synopsis: A Diwali fight. Whose parents this year. Eight years married, eight years of this exact fight. The therapist asks: 'What if neither of you is wrong?' They look at him like he is mad. Defensiveness is the body's fastest reflex; it is also the slowest path to being known.

episodes.title: The Story Watcher
episodes.synopsis: She watches all of his Instagram stories within ten minutes. He does not watch hers. He thinks she is being controlling. She is terrified. They both grew up with absent fathers — in different ways, with different consequences, in the same fight tonight. Goleman: attachment patterns set in the first three years come back, in disguise, on the fifteenth year of marriage.

episodes.title: You Don't Wear Sindoor
episodes.synopsis: She stopped wearing sindoor after her mother died. He has never told her how that small absence makes him feel — small, unchosen, not quite a husband. The fight has been every Sunday for two years. The work: separating her grief from his interpretation of it.

episodes.title: The Empty Chair
episodes.synopsis: She booked the session. He did not come. Dr. Mehta runs the session anyway, with the empty chair across from her. The empty chair tells him everything — about him, about her, about marriages where one person has already left while still living in the house.

episodes.title: We're Fine
episodes.synopsis: No fights. No tears. No nothing. They came because their teenage daughter said the silence at home was making her sick. Goleman would call this flatlining. The therapist calls it the most dangerous thing in the room — because the body has stopped trying to repair, and the mind has called it peace.

episodes.title: The Cousin's Wedding
episodes.synopsis: A same-sex couple, five years together. His cousin's wedding next month. Both sets of parents will be in the same room for the first time. They have not, yet, held hands at a family function. The session is a rehearsal — for the breath they will take before they walk in, together.

episodes.title: The Last Session
episodes.synopsis: Sometimes therapy is not repair. Sometimes it is acknowledgement. A couple decides — quietly, gently, with respect — that they are not going to make it. Dr. Mehta helps them say it without breaking each other. The hardest EQ skill: letting something end without making the other person the villain of your future story.

episodes.title: The Letter
episodes.synopsis: Goleman: forgiveness is what you do for yourself, not for them. A widow whose husband died with the fight unresolved. She comes alone. The session is a letter she will never send. Dr. Mehta sits with her while she writes the sentence she could not say in his lifetime. The empty chair is full again, briefly, the way grief allows.

episodes.title: Dr. Mehta at Home
episodes.synopsis: Dr. Kabir Mehta, alone in his clinic at 8 PM. Vrinda has called twice. He has not picked up. He opens his green Moleskine and writes one word — about himself. The series ends where it began: the only therapist in the room who can name the emotion he would rather not feel. The teacher, finally, does the homework.
